title: Topic 2 - Forces and Motion (LEH, U4)
subtitle: Vectors, motion graphs, Newton's first and second laws, the force–mass–acceleration practical, reaction time and estimation — the Topic 2 spec points taught in U4 (Edexcel GCSE Physics 1PH0)
lede: Everything in Topic 2, split into two bands. The non-negotiables are the facts and single-step calculations you must get right every time, without thinking. The tricky bits are where the marks are usually lost: multi-step calculations, explanations, and the ideas that look simple but have a trap in them. Each item is explained, shown in a worked example, then practised straight away.
howto: Start with the non-negotiables. Do not move on from a section until every practice question is green.
Read each explanation, then cover it and say it back to yourself. For an equation, write it out with every symbol labelled.
Study the worked example one step at a time and notice how the answer is laid out, not just what it is.
Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Write every calculation in EWAU layout on paper first, then type the answer to check it.
For "explain" questions, write your answer on paper in full sentences, then compare it with the model answer point by point before you mark yourself.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next — and what to ask about in class.

bands.title: The non-negotiables

bands.title: The tricky bits

bands.title: Key facts

sections.title: Scalars and vectors
sections.blurb: Every quantity in this topic is either a scalar or a vector. You must be able to say which is which, and why.
checklist: Define a scalar and a vector
Sort the spec's list of quantities into scalars and vectors
Explain that velocity is speed in a stated direction
Tell the difference between distance and displacement

parts.title: What makes a quantity a vector?
parts.html:
A scalar quantity has magnitude (size) only. A vector quantity has magnitude and a specific direction.

The exam expects you to know this list. The pairs are the ones that catch people out:

Scalar (size only)Vector (size and direction)
distancedisplacement
speedvelocity
massweight
energyforce
time, temperatureacceleration, momentum

Velocity is speed in a stated direction. "20 m/s" is a speed; "20 m/s due north" is a velocity. Two cars doing 20 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish, in a stated direction. Walk once round a running track and your distance is 400 m but your displacement is zero — you are back where you started.

parts.title: Distance, displacement, speed and velocity
parts.question: A ball is thrown and lands 12 m away from the thrower. Along its curved path it travels 15 m, taking 1.5 s. State the distance, the displacement, the average speed and the size of the average velocity.
steps: Distance is the length of the path actually travelled: 15 m.
Displacement is the straight line from start to finish: 12 m, in the direction of the throw.
Average velocity uses the displacement: $\text{velocity} = \dfrac{12}{1.5} = 8$ m/s in the direction of the throw.
Speed and velocity are different here because the path was not a straight line.

questions.text: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: Velocity has a direction (it is speed in a stated direction). Speed, distance and energy have size only.

questions.text: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
questions.explain: Mass has no direction — 5 kg is 5 kg whichever way you turn it. Force, weight and momentum all act in a direction.

questions.text: A car travels at 20 m/s due north. Which statement is correct?
options: 20 m/s is its velocity and 20 m/s due north is its speed
20 m/s is its speed and 20 m/s due north is its velocity
questions.explain: Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so adding "due north" turns the speed into a velocity.

questions.text: A student walks 30 m east along a corridor, then turns round and walks 10 m west.

parts.text: What distance has the student walked?
parts.hint: Distance is the total path length — add the two legs.
walkthrough: Distance $= 30 + 10 = 40$ m. Direction does not matter for a scalar.
parts.label: a

parts.text: What is the student's displacement from the start? (Give the size; the direction is east.)
parts.hint: Displacement is the straight line from start to finish. Walking back cancels some of it.
parts.label: b

questions.text: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 50 s.

parts.text: Calculate the runner's average speed.
parts.hint: Average speed uses the distance run.
parts.label: a

parts.text: State the runner's average velocity for the lap.
parts.hint: Where does the runner finish compared with where they started?
walkthrough: After one complete lap the runner is back at the start, so the displacement is 0 m.
parts.label: b

questions.text: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.
questions.model:
• Distance is the total length of the path travelled; it is a scalar.
  • Displacement is the straight-line distance from the start point to the finish point, in a stated direction; it is a vector.
  • A journey that returns to its start has a large distance but zero displacement.

sections.title: Speed, distance and time
sections.blurb: The speed equation, its two rearrangements, and the unit conversions that come with it (minutes, kilometres, km/h).
checklist: Use speed = distance ÷ time and rearrange it for distance or time
Convert minutes to seconds and kilometres to metres before calculating
Convert km/h to m/s
Find an average speed over a whole journey, including stops

parts.title: The equation and its rearrangements
parts.html:
$$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}\qquad v = \dfrac{x}{t}$$

Edexcel writes distance as $x$. Learn all three forms:

To find…Use…
speed$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$
distance$\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}$
time$\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

Units must match. In physics, work in metres and seconds so the speed comes out in m/s. Convert before you substitute: 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s, 1 km = 1000 m.

km/h → m/s: multiply by 1000 (km → m) and divide by 3600 (h → s). That is the same as dividing by 3.6. So 36 km/h = 10 m/s, and 72 km/h = 20 m/s.

Average speed over a journey is total distance ÷ total time — and the total time includes any time spent stopped.

parts.title: Converting km/h to m/s
parts.question: A train travels at 90 km/h. Calculate its speed in m/s.

parts.title: Speed, distance and time
parts.intro: Lay out every calculation in EWAU. Convert units first where you need to.

questions.text: A sprinter runs 150 m in 12 s. Calculate her average speed.
questions.hint: Distance divided by time.

questions.text: A cyclist rides at 8 m/s for 45 s. How far does he travel?
questions.hint: You want a distance, so multiply speed by time.

questions.text: A bus travels 2.4 km in 4 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
questions.hint: Convert 2.4 km to metres and 4 minutes to seconds first.

questions.text: Sound travels through air at 340 m/s. How long does thunder take to reach you from a lightning strike 1.7 km away?
questions.hint: Convert 1.7 km to metres, then divide the distance by the speed.

questions.text: A car travels at 108 km/h on a motorway. Calculate its speed in m/s.
questions.hint: 108 km is 108 000 m, and 1 hour is 3600 s.

questions.text: A delivery rider covers 600 m in 60 s, waits 30 s at a crossing, then covers another 300 m in 60 s. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
questions.hint: Total distance over total time — and the 30 s wait counts in the total time.
walkthrough: Total distance $= 600 + 300 = 900$ m. Total time $= 60 + 30 + 60 = 150$ s.

sections.title: Acceleration
sections.blurb: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. The sign matters: slowing down is a negative acceleration.
checklist: Use a = (v − u) ÷ t, with u the initial and v the final velocity
Give a deceleration as a negative acceleration
Rearrange to find a final velocity or a time

parts.title: Change in velocity ÷ time
parts.html:
$$\text{acceleration} = \dfrac{\text{change in velocity}}{\text{time taken}}\qquad a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$$

Here $u$ is the initial velocity ("u comes before v in the alphabet") and $v$ is the final velocity. The unit of acceleration is m/s²: metres per second, every second.

An acceleration of 3 m/s² means the velocity increases by 3 m/s each second: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 …

Slowing down gives a negative answer, because $v$ is smaller than $u$. That is called a deceleration. If a question says "include the sign" or "calculate the acceleration" of something slowing down, write the minus sign.

To find…Use…
acceleration$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$
final velocity$v = u + a \times t$
time$t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$

parts.title: Calculating an acceleration
parts.question: A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 20 m/s in 6 s. Calculate its acceleration.

questions.text: A motorbike accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 4 s. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: "From rest" means u = 0.

questions.text: A lorry slows from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. Calculate its acceleration. Include the sign.
questions.hint: v is smaller than u, so the top of the fraction is negative.

questions.text: A boat moving at 4 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Calculate its final velocity.
questions.hint: Rearrange for v: the velocity gained is a × t, added on to u.

questions.text: A train accelerates at 1.5 m/s² from 10 m/s to 25 m/s. How long does this take?
questions.hint: Find the change in velocity first, then divide by the acceleration.

questions.text: A car travelling at 24 m/s decelerates at 6 m/s² for 3 s. Calculate its velocity at the end of the 3 s.
questions.hint: A deceleration of 6 m/s² is an acceleration of −6 m/s².

questions.text: A trolley released from rest on a ramp reaches 1.2 m/s after 0.8 s. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: u = 0 because it starts from rest.

sections.title: v² − u² = 2ax
sections.blurb: The equation for when you know a distance but not a time. Substitute, then rearrange — and remember the square root at the end.
checklist: Recognise when to use v² − u² = 2ax (no time given, or no time wanted)
Substitute into it and solve for v, u, a or x
Remember to square-root when the unknown is a velocity

parts.title: When there is no time in the question
parts.html:
$$v^2 - u^2 = 2 \times a \times x$$

$u$ = initial velocity, $v$ = final velocity, $a$ = acceleration, $x$ = distance travelled. There is no $t$ in this equation, so use it whenever the question gives you (or asks for) a distance and says nothing about time.

Safest method: substitute the numbers first, then rearrange. Square the velocities before you do anything else.

Finding…Do this
$v$$v^2 = u^2 + 2ax$, then square-root
$a$$a = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2x}$
$x$$x = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$

For an object falling freely, $a = g = 10$ m/s². For something stopping, $v = 0$ and $a$ is negative.

parts.title: Finding a final velocity
parts.question: A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates at 3 m/s² over a distance of 24 m. Calculate her final velocity.
steps: $u = 0$, $a = 3$ m/s², $x = 24$ m. No time is mentioned, so use $v^2 - u^2 = 2ax$.

questions.text: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 16 m. Calculate its final velocity.
questions.hint: u = 0. Work out v² first, then square-root.

questions.text: A runner moving at 5 m/s accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 20 m. Calculate her final velocity.
questions.hint: Square u (5² = 25) before adding 2ax.

questions.text: A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes and stops in 50 m. Calculate its acceleration. Include the sign.
questions.hint: Stopping means v = 0. The answer is negative.

questions.text: A lorry travelling at 30 m/s decelerates at 6 m/s² until it stops. Calculate the distance it travels while stopping.
questions.hint: v = 0 and a = −6 m/s². Two negatives on the fraction give a positive distance.

questions.text: A stone is dropped from a bridge 20 m above a river. Calculate its speed as it hits the water. (Ignore air resistance; g = 10 m/s².)
questions.hint: Dropped means u = 0, and the acceleration is g = 10 m/s².

questions.text: A car accelerates at 2 m/s² over 100 m and reaches 25 m/s. Calculate its initial velocity.
questions.hint: This time v is known and u is the unknown: u² = v² − 2ax.

sections.title: Distance–time graphs
sections.blurb: The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed. Flat means stationary; steeper means faster.
checklist: Read the speed from the gradient of a straight section
Recognise a stationary section (horizontal line)
Compare speeds from steepness
Find an average speed for a whole journey from the graph

parts.title: Gradient means speed
parts.html:
On a distance–time graph, gradient = speed. Draw a big triangle on the straight section, then:

$$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}$$
Shape of lineMotion
Straight, sloping upConstant speed
Horizontal (flat)Stationary — distance is not changing
Steeper straight lineFaster constant speed
Straight, sloping downConstant speed back towards the start (if the axis is distance from the start)
CurvedChanging speed — see the tricky bits

Use the whole straight section for your triangle: bigger triangles give more accurate gradients.

parts.title: Speed from a gradient
parts.question: The graph shows a walker's journey. Calculate the walker's speed between 0 and 20 s.

graph.alt: Distance–time graph: rises to 200 m at 20 s, flat until 40 s, then rises to 300 m at 60 s.

steps: Between $t = 0$ and $t = 20$ s the line is straight, so the speed is constant. Draw a triangle from the origin to point A.
Change in distance $= 200 - 0 = 200$ m. Change in time $= 20 - 0 = 20$ s.

questions.text: Use the walker's graph from the worked example.

parts.text: Calculate the walker's speed between B and C (40 s to 60 s).
parts.hint: Distance goes from 200 m to 300 m while time goes from 40 s to 60 s.
parts.label: a

parts.text: What is the walker doing between A and B (20 s to 40 s)?
parts.explain: The line is horizontal: the distance stays at 200 m, so the walker is not moving.
parts.label: b

parts.text: What total distance did the walker travel in the 60 s?
parts.hint: Read the final distance off the graph.
walkthrough: At 60 s the distance from the start is 300 m, and the walker never came back, so the total distance is 300 m.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Calculate the walker's average speed for the whole 60 s.
parts.hint: Total distance ÷ total time, including the 20 s stop.
parts.label: d

graph.alt: Distance–time graph: rises to 200 m at 20 s, flat until 40 s, then rises to 300 m at 60 s.

questions.text: The graph shows the distance of a cyclist from her front door.

parts.text: Calculate the cyclist's speed during the first 30 s.
parts.hint: Gradient of the first straight section.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Which section of the journey was the fastest?
options: They were all the same speed
parts.explain: The steepest line is the fastest. The return leg covers 150 m in only 20 s; the outward leg took 30 s for the same distance.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate her speed on the way back (50 s to 70 s).
parts.hint: Ignore the minus sign on the gradient: a downward slope still has a speed.
walkthrough: Distance from the door changes from 150 m to 0 in $70 - 50 = 20$ s.
The gradient is negative because she is coming back towards the door; the steepness gives the speed and the sign gives the direction.
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Distance-from-start against time for a cyclist: rises to 150 m at 30 s, flat until 50 s, then falls back to 0 at 70 s.

sections.title: Velocity–time graphs
sections.blurb: Gradient gives acceleration; area under the line gives distance. Rectangles and triangles — and keep the units straight.
checklist: Find an acceleration from the gradient of a straight section
Recognise constant velocity (horizontal) and deceleration (sloping down)
Find a distance from the area under the line (rectangle or triangle)

parts.title: Gradient for acceleration, area for distance
parts.html:
A velocity–time graph tells you two things:

FeatureGives youHow
GradientAccelerationchange in velocity ÷ change in time (a triangle on the line)
Area under the lineDistance travelledsplit into rectangles and triangles, add them up

Reading the shape: a line sloping up is acceleration; horizontal is constant velocity (zero acceleration, so zero resultant force); sloping down is deceleration.

Areas: rectangle $= \text{base} \times \text{height}$; triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$. The base is a time and the height is a velocity, so the area comes out in metres.

Do not mix the two graphs up: on a distance–time graph the gradient is speed; on a velocity–time graph the gradient is acceleration.

parts.title: Acceleration and distance from a v–t graph
parts.question: The graph shows a tram's journey between two stops. Calculate (a) the acceleration in the first 10 s and (b) the distance travelled in the first 10 s.

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph: rises from 0 to 20 m/s at 10 s, flat until 20 s, falls to 0 at 30 s.

steps: (a) Gradient from the origin to P: velocity changes by $20 - 0 = 20$ m/s in $10 - 0 = 10$ s.
(b) The area under the line from 0 to 10 s is a triangle with base 10 s and height 20 m/s.

questions.text: Use the tram's graph from the worked example.

parts.text: Calculate the tram's acceleration between 20 s and 30 s. Include the sign.
parts.hint: The velocity falls from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled between P and Q (10 s to 20 s).
parts.hint: That part of the area is a rectangle: 10 s wide and 20 m/s tall.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the total distance between the two stops.
parts.hint: Triangle + rectangle + triangle.
parts.label: c

parts.text: During which part of the journey is the resultant force on the tram zero?
parts.explain: Between P and Q the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero — and Newton's first law says the resultant force is zero.
parts.label: d

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph: rises from 0 to 20 m/s at 10 s, flat until 20 s, falls to 0 at 30 s.

questions.text: The graph shows a car joining a dual carriageway.

parts.text: Calculate the car's acceleration in the first 8 s.
parts.hint: It does not start from rest: u = 5 m/s.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled between 8 s and 12 s.
parts.hint: A rectangle 4 s wide and 25 m/s tall.
parts.label: b

sections.title: Typical speeds and g
sections.blurb: Numbers you must simply know: everyday speeds, the acceleration of free fall, and the size of everyday accelerations.
checklist: Recall typical speeds for walking, running, cycling, cars, trains, wind and sound
Recall that g = 10 m/s² in free fall
Estimate the size of everyday accelerations

parts.title: Speeds and accelerations to memorise
parts.html:
Exam questions ask you to recall these, or to spot a silly answer (a cyclist at 60 m/s is not plausible). Learn the rough values:

Moving thingTypical speed
Walkingabout 1.5 m/s
Runningabout 3 m/s (a sprinter: 10 m/s)
Cyclingabout 6 m/s
Car in town (30 mph)about 13 m/s
Car on a motorway (70 mph)about 30 m/s
Fast trainabout 55 m/s
Airlinerabout 250 m/s
Windlight breeze 5 m/s; gale 20 m/s
Sound in airabout 340 m/s

Free fall: near the Earth's surface, anything falling freely accelerates at $g = 10$ m/s² (ignoring air resistance). Its speed increases by 10 m/s every second.

Everyday accelerationRough size
Lift starting to moveabout 1 m/s²
Family car pulling away2–3 m/s²
Sprinter off the blocksabout 5 m/s²
Free fall10 m/s²
Car in a crashhundreds of m/s²

parts.title: Using g
parts.question: A coin is dropped down a well. Calculate its speed after 2 s of free fall.
steps: Dropped means $u = 0$. In free fall $a = g = 10$ m/s², $t = 2$ s.
Sense check: 20 m/s is about 45 mph — fast, but plausible for 2 s of falling.

questions.text: Which is the best estimate of walking speed?
questions.explain: About 1.5 m/s — roughly 5 km/h. 15 m/s would be faster than an Olympic sprinter.

questions.text: What is the approximate speed of sound in air?
questions.explain: About 340 m/s. The last option is the speed of light.

questions.text: A car is driving along a motorway. Which is the best estimate of its speed?
questions.explain: 70 mph is about 30 m/s. 13 m/s is the 30 mph town limit.

questions.text: A ball is dropped from a tall building. Calculate its speed after 3 s. (Ignore air resistance.)
questions.hint: It gains 10 m/s every second.

questions.text: A stone is dropped from a cliff. Calculate its speed after 1.5 s.
questions.hint: v = u + at with u = 0 and a = 10 m/s².

questions.text: Which is the best estimate of the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights?
questions.explain: About 2 m/s²: 0 to 13 m/s (30 mph) in roughly 6 s. 20 m/s² is twice the acceleration of free fall — you would be pinned to your seat.

sections.title: Measuring speed in the lab
sections.blurb: Light gates, stopwatches, ticker timers and video: what each one actually measures, and the calculation that turns it into a speed.
equations: \text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{length of card}}{\text{time to pass through gate}}
checklist: Describe how to measure a speed with a light gate and an interrupt card
Describe how to measure a speed with a stopwatch and a metre rule
Explain why light gates give more accurate timings than a stopwatch

parts.title: Every method measures a distance and a time
parts.html:
No instrument measures speed directly. Each method measures a distance and a time, and you calculate speed = distance ÷ time.

MethodDistanceTimeNotes
Stopwatch + metre rule / tapeMarked out on the floor or benchStopwatch, started and stopped by handSimple, but human reaction time (about 0.2 s) adds error. Fine for long times; poor for anything under a few seconds.
One light gate + interrupt cardLength of the card on the trolleyHow long the card blocks the beamGives the speed at that point. The timer starts and stops automatically, so no reaction time.
Two light gatesDistance between the gatesTime for the trolley to go from one gate to the otherGives the average speed between the gates.
Ticker timerMeasured between dots on the tape50 dots per second, so 0.02 s between dotsOlder method; dots spreading out shows acceleration.
Video / motion sensorScale in the frame, or ultrasound pulsesFrame rate, or the sensor's clockRecords the whole motion, not just one moment.

For a light gate: $$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{length of card}}{\text{time to pass through gate}}$$ Convert the card length to metres.

parts.title: Speed from a light gate
parts.question: A trolley carries a card 5.0 cm long. The card takes 0.025 s to pass through a light gate. Calculate the trolley's speed.
steps: Convert the card length: $5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.050$ m.
Equation: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{length of card}}{\text{time to pass through gate}}$

questions.text: A 10 cm card on a trolley blocks a light gate for 0.040 s. Calculate the speed of the trolley.
walkthrough: Equation: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{length of card}}{\text{time to pass through gate}}$

questions.text: Two light gates are placed 0.80 m apart. A trolley takes 0.32 s to travel from the first gate to the second. Calculate its average speed between the gates.
questions.hint: Distance between the gates ÷ time between the gates.

questions.text: Explain why a light gate gives a more accurate speed than a student with a stopwatch.
questions.model:
• The light gate's timer starts and stops automatically when the beam is broken.
  • So there is no human reaction time (about 0.2 s) adding to the measured time.
  • This matters most when the time being measured is short — the error from reaction time would be a large fraction of it.

questions.text: What does a light gate connected to a timer measure directly?
questions.explain: It measures a time: how long the beam is broken. You have to divide a distance (the card length) by that time to get a speed.

questions.text: A student uses a stopwatch to time a toy car travelling 1.5 m along a bench. The time is 2.5 s. Calculate the average speed.
questions.hint: Distance over time, nothing to convert.

questions.text: Describe how you would measure the speed of a trolley at one point on a bench using a light gate.
questions.model:
• Fix a card of known length to the trolley and measure the card's length with a ruler.
  • Set up the light gate at the point of interest, connected to a timer, so the card breaks the beam as the trolley passes.
  • Read the time the beam is blocked from the timer.
  • Calculate speed = length of card ÷ time. Repeat and take a mean.

sections.title: Newton's first law and resultant force
sections.blurb: Find the resultant of forces along a line, then say what it does: zero resultant keeps the motion as it is; a non-zero resultant changes it.
equations: \text{resultant force} = \text{forces one way} - \text{forces the other way}
checklist: State Newton's first law
Calculate a resultant force from two forces along a line
Say what happens when the resultant force is zero, and when it is not

parts.title: Resultant force and what it does
parts.html:
The resultant force is the single force that would have the same effect as all the forces acting together. For forces along one line: add the ones pointing the same way, subtract the ones pointing the opposite way.

Newton's first law: an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity (same speed, same direction), unless a resultant force acts on it.

Resultant forceWhat happens
Zero (forces balanced)Stationary object stays still; moving object keeps the same velocity
Not zero, same direction as motionSpeeds up
Not zero, opposite to motionSlows down
Not zero, at an angle to motionChanges direction

The common mistake: thinking a moving object needs a force to keep it moving. It does not. A car at a steady 20 m/s has a driving force exactly balanced by friction and air resistance — the resultant is zero.

parts.title: Resultant force on a car
parts.question: A car's engine provides a forward force of 3000 N. Friction and air resistance total 2200 N. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Describe the car's motion. (c) Air resistance increases until the backward forces total 3000 N. Describe the motion now.
steps: (b) The resultant is not zero and is in the direction of motion, so the car accelerates (speeds up).
(c) Now $\text{resultant} = 3000 - 3000 = 0$ N. The forces are balanced, so by Newton's first law the car continues at a constant velocity.
It does not stop — a zero resultant force means no change in motion.

questions.text: A sledge is pulled forwards with a force of 450 N while friction of 300 N acts backwards. Calculate the resultant force.
questions.hint: Subtract the backward force from the forward force.
walkthrough: Equation: $\text{resultant force} = \text{forces one way} - \text{forces the other way}$

questions.text: A parachutist is falling at a constant velocity. What can you say about the forces on her?
options: Her weight is bigger than the air resistance
The air resistance is bigger than her weight
Her weight and the air resistance are equal in size
questions.explain: Constant velocity means zero resultant force (Newton's first law), so the upward air resistance exactly balances her weight.

questions.text: A helicopter's rotor provides 2000 N of lift. The helicopter weighs 1500 N. Calculate the resultant force.
questions.hint: Up minus down.
walkthrough: Equation: $\text{resultant force} = \text{forces one way} - \text{forces the other way}$

questions.text: A boat's engine pushes it forwards with 5000 N. The water resistance is also 5000 N. State the resultant force on the boat.
questions.hint: The forces are equal and opposite.
walkthrough: The boat continues at a constant velocity.

questions.text: State Newton's first law of motion.
questions.model:
• An object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object continues at a constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line),
  • unless a resultant force acts on it.

questions.text: An ice puck slides at 8 m/s across perfectly smooth ice with no resultant force on it. What happens to it?
options: It keeps moving at 8 m/s in a straight line
questions.explain: No resultant force means no change in velocity. It carries on at 8 m/s until something pushes on it.

sections.title: Newton's second law: F = ma
sections.blurb: Resultant force, mass and acceleration — with the unit conversions (grams, kilonewtons) and one two-step question.
checklist: Use F = ma and rearrange it for m or a
Convert grams to kilograms and kN to N before substituting
Remember that F is the resultant force

parts.title: Force, mass and acceleration
parts.html:
$$F = m \times a$$

$F$ is the resultant force in newtons, $m$ the mass in kilograms, $a$ the acceleration in m/s². A bigger force gives a bigger acceleration; a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration for the same force.

To find…Use…
force$F = m \times a$
acceleration$a = \dfrac{F}{m}$
mass$m = \dfrac{F}{a}$

Units: 500 g = 0.5 kg; 2.5 kN = 2500 N; 1 tonne = 1000 kg. Convert before you substitute.

If a question gives two forces, find the resultant first (the tricky bits cover this), then use $F = ma$ with the resultant.

parts.title: Finding an acceleration
parts.question: A car of mass 1200 kg experiences a resultant force of 3000 N. Calculate its acceleration.

questions.text: A resultant force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg trolley. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: a = F ÷ m.

questions.text: A car of mass 800 kg accelerates at 2 m/s². Calculate the resultant force on it.
questions.hint: Multiply mass by acceleration.

questions.text: A resultant force of 60 N gives a box an acceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate the mass of the box.
questions.hint: m = F ÷ a.

questions.text: A resultant force of 2 N acts on a 500 g model car. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: Convert 500 g to kilograms first.

A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 8 m/s in 2 s.

parts.text: Calculate the sprinter's acceleration.
parts.hint: Change in velocity ÷ time.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the resultant force on the sprinter.
parts.hint: Use the acceleration you just found in F = ma.

sections.title: Weight, mass and g
sections.blurb: Weight is a force; mass is not. W = mg links them through the gravitational field strength, which is different on different planets.
checklist: Define weight and use W = mg
Explain the difference between mass and weight
Describe how weight is measured
Describe how weight depends on gravitational field strength

parts.title: Mass is not weight
parts.html:
MassWeight
What it isThe amount of matter in an objectThe force of gravity pulling the object towards the Earth (or planet)
Unitkilograms, kgnewtons, N
Scalar or vector?ScalarVector — it acts downwards, towards the centre of the planet
On the Moon…Same as on EarthAbout one sixth of the Earth value
Measured withA balance (compares against known masses)A newtonmeter (a calibrated spring balance)
$$W = m \times g$$

$g$ is the gravitational field strength, in N/kg: the force of gravity on each kilogram. On Earth $g = 10$ N/kg. (The same number as the acceleration of free fall, 10 m/s² — not a coincidence.)

Place$g$ / N/kg
Earth10
Moon1.6
Mars3.7
Jupiter25

Weight is directly proportional to $g$. Take the same mass somewhere with twice the field strength and it weighs twice as much.

parts.title: Weight on Earth and on the Moon
parts.question: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. Calculate her weight (a) on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and (b) on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg).
steps: (b) Her mass is still 60 kg on the Moon. $W = 60 \times 1.6 = 96$ N.
Her weight on the Moon is 96 N, about one sixth of 600 N, because $g$ is about one sixth as big.

questions.text: Calculate the weight of a 12 kg suitcase on Earth.
questions.hint: W = mg with g = 10 N/kg.

questions.text: A person weighs 350 N on Earth. Calculate their mass.
questions.hint: Rearrange: m = W ÷ g.

questions.text: A 50 kg rover lands on Mars, where g = 3.7 N/kg. Calculate its weight on Mars.
questions.hint: Use the Mars value of g, not 10.

questions.text: A 5 kg mass weighs 125 N on a certain planet. Calculate the planet's gravitational field strength.
questions.hint: g = W ÷ m.

questions.text: An astronaut travels from the Earth to the Moon. What happens to her mass?
options: It decreases to about one sixth
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter in her body — it does not depend on where she is. Her weight falls to about one sixth.

questions.text: Describe how the weight of an object can be measured.
questions.model:
• Hang the object from a newtonmeter (a calibrated spring balance) and read the force in newtons directly.
  • Or: measure the mass on a balance, then calculate W = m × g.

sections.title: Core practical: force, mass and acceleration
sections.blurb: The method you must be able to describe: a trolley, a string over a pulley, hanging masses, light gates. The analysis is in the tricky bits.
checklist: Describe the equipment and method of the trolley core practical
Name the independent, dependent and control variables
Calculate the accelerating force from the hanging mass

parts.title: The method
parts.html:
Aim: investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the force applied and on its mass.

Set-up: a trolley on a runway (bench or ramp); a string from the trolley over a pulley at the end of the bench to a mass hanger; a card on the trolley and two light gates connected to a data logger; a set of slotted masses.

StepDetail
1Measure the length of the card. Measure the distance between the light gates.
2Hang a mass on the hanger. The weight of the hanging mass is the force pulling the trolley: $F = m \times g$.
3Release the trolley from the same starting point each time. The data logger records the speed at each gate and the time between them, and calculates the acceleration.
4 (force)Move one slotted mass from the trolley to the hanger and repeat, so the force changes but the total mass being accelerated stays the same.
4 (mass)Or: keep the hanging mass the same and add masses to the trolley, so the mass changes but the force stays the same.
5Repeat each reading three times and take a mean. Plot acceleration against force (or against mass).
Investigating forceInvestigating mass
Independent: force (hanging weight)Independent: total mass
Dependent: accelerationDependent: acceleration
Control: total mass of trolley + hanger, same runway, same starting pointControl: force (hanging mass), same runway, same starting point

parts.title: The force from a hanging mass
parts.question: In the experiment a 100 g mass hangs from the string. The trolley, card and hanging mass have a total mass of 1.2 kg. Calculate (a) the force accelerating the trolley and (b) the expected acceleration.
steps: (a) The force is the weight of the hanging mass. $100 \text{ g} = 0.1$ kg, so $F = 0.1 \times 10 = 1.0$ N.
(b) This force accelerates everything attached to the string: the trolley and the hanging mass, 1.2 kg in total.

questions.text: A 200 g mass is hung from the string. Calculate the force pulling the trolley.
questions.hint: Weight of the hanging mass: convert to kg, multiply by 10.

questions.text: The total mass of the trolley and the hanging mass is 0.8 kg. Using the force from question 1, calculate the expected acceleration.
questions.hint: a = F ÷ (total mass).

questions.text: A student investigates how acceleration depends on force. What is the independent variable?
questions.explain: The independent variable is the one the student deliberately changes — the force, by moving masses onto the hanger. Acceleration is the dependent variable.

questions.text: When investigating force, where should the extra masses come from when you increase the hanging mass?
questions.explain: Moving a mass from the trolley to the hanger increases the force while keeping the total accelerated mass constant. Adding masses from elsewhere would change two variables at once.

questions.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of force on the acceleration of a trolley.
questions.model:
• Trolley on a bench, string over a pulley to a mass hanger; card on the trolley; two light gates and a data logger.
  • The hanging weight provides the force (F = mg); the data logger measures the speed at each gate and the time between them, giving the acceleration.
  • Change the force by moving a slotted mass from the trolley to the hanger, so the total mass stays constant.
  • Repeat each force three times, take a mean, and plot acceleration against force.

questions.text: Which graph would you expect for acceleration against force (with the mass constant)?
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a negative gradient
questions.explain: F = ma means a is directly proportional to F: doubling the force doubles the acceleration, so the graph is a straight line through the origin. Its gradient is 1/m.

sections.title: Motion graphs the hard way
sections.blurb: Areas that are not simple triangles, graphs that go below the axis, and turning a shape into a sentence (or a sentence into a shape).
checklist: Find the area under a section that isn't a simple triangle or rectangle (trapezium, or rectangle + triangle)
Interpret a negative velocity on a velocity–time graph
Tell displacement from distance when the graph goes below the axis
Describe the motion shown by a graph in words, and sketch a graph from a description

parts.title: Three things that catch people out
parts.html:
1. When the section isn't a simple triangle or rectangle. If a sloping line starts above the time axis — say the velocity goes from 10 m/s up to 20 m/s — the area under it is a trapezium. Either use $\tfrac{1}{2}(a + b) \times h$ with $a$ and $b$ the two parallel sides (the velocity at the start and at the end of the section) and $h$ the time it lasts, or split it into a rectangle (the lower velocity × time) with a triangle sitting on top.

2. Velocity below the axis. A negative velocity means the object is moving in the opposite direction — not slowing down. The line passing through zero is the moment it changes direction. Area below the axis is distance travelled backwards: add it for total distance, subtract it for displacement.

3. Converting between the two graphs.

MotionDistance–time graphVelocity–time graph
StationaryHorizontal lineLine along the time axis (v = 0)
Constant velocityStraight line, slopingHorizontal line above the axis
Constant acceleration from restCurve getting steeperStraight line sloping up from the origin
Constant deceleration to restCurve flattening outStraight line sloping down to the axis
Returning to the startLine sloping back down to zeroLine below the axis

To describe motion from a graph, go section by section: name the motion, give the numbers (how fast, how long, how far), and say when it changes.

parts.title: Area of a trapezium
parts.question: The graph shows a van's velocity. Calculate the distance travelled in the first 10 s (the shaded region).

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph starting at 10 m/s, rising to 20 m/s at 10 s, constant to 20 s, falling to zero at 30 s.

steps: The shaded region is a trapezium: parallel sides 10 m/s (at $t = 0$) and 20 m/s (at $t = 10$ s), width 10 s.
Method 2: rectangle $10 \times 10 = 100$ m, plus triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10 = 50$ m, total $150$ m.
Distance in the first 10 s $= 150$ m. (Forgetting the rectangle underneath and answering 50 m is the classic error.)

questions.text: Use the van's graph from the worked example.

parts.text: Calculate the total distance the van travels in the 30 s.
parts.hint: Trapezium + rectangle + triangle.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Describe the motion of the van during the 30 s. Use numbers from the graph.
parts.model:
• 0–10 s: the van is already moving at 10 m/s and accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s (acceleration 1 m/s²).
  • 10–20 s: constant velocity of 20 m/s (zero acceleration, zero resultant force).
  • 20–30 s: decelerates uniformly from 20 m/s to rest (acceleration −2 m/s²), stopping at 30 s.
parts.label: b

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph starting at 10 m/s, rising to 20 m/s at 10 s, constant to 20 s, falling to zero at 30 s.

questions.text: The graph shows the velocity of a remote-controlled car along a straight track. Forwards is positive.

parts.text: Calculate the distance the car travels forwards in the first 6 s.
parts.hint: Triangle + rectangle + triangle, all above the axis.
walkthrough: Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10$ m; rectangle $2 \times 10 = 20$ m; triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10$ m.
parts.label: a

parts.text: What is the car doing between 6 s and 8 s?
options: Slowing down while still moving forwards
parts.explain: The velocity is negative, so the car is moving in the opposite direction. It reverses, fastest at 7 s, and comes to rest at 8 s.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the car's displacement from its starting point at 8 s.
parts.hint: Area above the axis minus area below it.
walkthrough: Area below the axis (6–8 s): triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10$ m backwards.
Displacement $= 40 - 10 = 30$ m forwards of the start.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Calculate the total distance the car travels in the 8 s.
parts.hint: For distance, every bit of area counts, whichever side of the axis.
parts.label: d

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph: rises to 10 m/s at 2 s, constant until 4 s, falls through zero at 6 s to −10 m/s at 7 s, back to zero at 8 s.

questions.text: An object's velocity–time graph is a horizontal line above the time axis. What does its distance–time graph look like?
questions.explain: Constant velocity means the distance increases by the same amount every second — a straight sloping line on a distance–time graph.

questions.text: A distance–time graph is a curve that gets steeper and steeper. What does the velocity–time graph look like?
options: A line along the time axis
questions.explain: Getting steeper means the speed is increasing. If it increases steadily, the velocity–time graph is a straight line sloping up.

sections.title: Curved graphs and tangents
sections.blurb: A curve means the gradient is changing. To find the speed (or acceleration) at one instant, draw a tangent and take its gradient.
equations: \text{instantaneous speed} = \text{gradient of tangent to } x\text{–}t \text{ graph}
checklist: Recognise speeding up and slowing down from the shape of a curved distance–time graph
Find an instantaneous speed from the gradient of a tangent to a distance–time graph
Find an acceleration at an instant from the gradient of a tangent to a velocity–time graph
Describe how the acceleration changes when a velocity–time graph curves

parts.title: Reading a curve
parts.html:
On a straight line the gradient is the same everywhere. On a curve the gradient changes from point to point, so the speed (on a distance–time graph) or the acceleration (on a velocity–time graph) is changing.

Curve shapeDistance–time graphVelocity–time graph
Getting steeperSpeeding upAcceleration increasing
Flattening out (bending towards horizontal)Slowing downAcceleration decreasing (velocity still rising, but more slowly)
HorizontalStationaryConstant velocity, zero acceleration

To find the value at one instant, draw a tangent: a straight line that just touches the curve at that point, with the same steepness as the curve there. Then find the gradient of the tangent with a large triangle, reading its ends off gridline intersections.

Pick the triangle's corners from the tangent, not from the curve — the whole point is that the curve's gradient is different everywhere else.

parts.title: What a tangent is not
parts.html: The gradient of the line from the origin to a point on the curve is the average speed up to that time, not the speed at that instant. Only a tangent gives the instantaneous value. On the graph below, the chord from the origin to P would give $18 \div 6 = 3$ m/s — the average — while the tangent gives $6$ m/s, the actual speed at $t = 6$ s.

parts.title: Instantaneous speed from a tangent
parts.question: The graph shows the distance travelled by a sprinter leaving the blocks. The tangent at P (t = 6 s) is drawn. Calculate the sprinter's speed at 6 s.

graph.alt: Distance–time graph curving upwards (accelerating), with a tangent drawn at t = 6 s from (3, 0) to (8, 30).

steps: The tangent at P passes through $(3,\ 0)$ and $(8,\ 30)$ — read where it crosses gridline intersections.
Change in distance $= 30 - 0 = 30$ m. Change in time $= 8 - 3 = 5$ s.
The curve gets steeper as time goes on, so the sprinter is speeding up: her speed at 6 s (6 m/s) is more than her average so far (3 m/s).

questions.text: The graph shows the distance travelled by a car as it slows down for a junction. The tangent at Q (t = 4 s) is drawn.

parts.text: How can you tell from the shape of the graph that the car is slowing down?
options: The curve gets flatter (less steep) as time goes on
parts.explain: The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed. The curve flattens out, so the gradient — and the speed — is decreasing.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Use the tangent to calculate the car's speed at Q.
parts.hint: The tangent passes through (2, 40) and (7, 100).
parts.label: b

parts.text: At what time does the car stop?
parts.explain: The car is stationary when the distance stops changing — where the curve becomes horizontal, at 10 s.
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Distance–time graph curving over and flattening out at t = 10 s (decelerating), with a tangent at t = 4 s from (2, 40) to (7, 100).

questions.text: The graph shows the velocity of a skydiver after jumping from a plane. The tangent at t = 0 is drawn.

parts.text: Use the tangent to calculate the skydiver's acceleration at the moment of jumping.
parts.hint: The tangent goes from (0, 0) to (5, 20).
walkthrough: (With air resistance ignored this would be 10 m/s²; the skydiver's suit and the thin plane air give a smaller value in this example.)
parts.label: a

parts.text: How does the skydiver's acceleration change during the 20 s?
parts.explain: The curve flattens: the gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration, and it drops towards zero as the velocity approaches 20 m/s.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Explain, in terms of forces, why the graph has this shape.
parts.model:
• At first air resistance is small, so there is a large resultant force (weight − air resistance) downwards and a large acceleration.
  • As the velocity increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease.
  • Eventually air resistance equals the weight; the resultant force is zero and the velocity is constant: terminal velocity (20 m/s here).
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph rising steeply at first then levelling off towards 20 m/s, with a tangent at the origin from (0, 0) to (5, 20) and a dashed line at 20 m/s.

questions.text: Describe how to find the instantaneous speed of an object at a particular time from a curved distance–time graph.
questions.model:
• Draw a tangent to the curve at that time: a straight line that touches the curve there with the same steepness.
  • Draw a large triangle on the tangent, using points where it crosses gridlines.
  • Speed = gradient of the tangent = change in distance ÷ change in time.

sections.title: Choosing the equation, and the sign of a
sections.blurb: When a question mixes velocities, accelerations, times and distances: list what you know, pick the equation that fits, and keep the minus signs honest.
checklist: List u, v, a, t and x, and pick the equation that contains the three you know and the one you want
Use a negative acceleration for an object slowing down, and v = 0 for an object stopping
Chain two equations: find one quantity, then use it in the next step

parts.title: List the five, pick the equation
parts.html:
Every motion question involves some of five quantities. Write them down with values before you choose anything:

SymbolQuantityClues in the question
$u$initial velocity"from rest" → $u = 0$; "travelling at"
$v$final velocity"stops" / "comes to rest" → $v = 0$; at the top of a throw → $v = 0$
$a$acceleration"decelerates at" → negative; "falls freely" → $10$ m/s²
$t$timeseconds, minutes (convert)
$x$distance"over a distance of", "in 50 m", height fallen
You have / wantEquation
$u, v, a, t$ (no distance)$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$
$u, v, a, x$ (no time)$v^2 - u^2 = 2ax$
$t$ and $x$ both involvedTwo steps: use one equation to find $v$ or $a$, then the other (or use a velocity–time graph)

Signs. Choose the direction of motion as positive. Then a deceleration is a negative $a$, and anything pointing the other way is negative. In $v^2 - u^2 = 2ax$ the squares are always positive, so a stopping object gives a negative top line and a negative $a$ — the distance comes out positive, as it should.

parts.title: A stopping car, two questions
parts.question: A car travelling at 24 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate (a) the distance it travels before stopping and (b) the time it takes to stop.
steps: List: $u = 24$ m/s, $v = 0$ (stops), $a = -4$ m/s² (decelerating). Wanted: $x$ in (a), $t$ in (b).
Check with the graph picture: a triangle of height 24 m/s and base 6 s has area $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 24 = 72$ m. ✓

questions.text: A lorry travelling at 18 m/s brakes and stops in a distance of 27 m. Calculate its acceleration. Include the sign.
questions.hint: You have u, v (= 0) and x, so there is no time: use v² − u² = 2ax.

questions.text: A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates at 1.2 m/s² along 60 m of straight road.

parts.text: Calculate her velocity at the end of the 60 m.
parts.hint: No time is given: v² = u² + 2ax with u = 0.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate how long the 60 m takes.
parts.hint: Now you know v, use a = (v − u)/t rearranged for t.
parts.label: b

questions.text: A question gives the initial velocity, the acceleration and the distance, and asks for the final velocity. Which equation should you use?
questions.explain: No time is given or wanted, so the equation without t is the one: v² − u² = 2ax.

questions.text: A ball is thrown straight up at 15 m/s. Calculate the maximum height it reaches. (g = 10 m/s²; ignore air resistance.)
questions.hint: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, v = 0. Taking up as positive, a = −10 m/s².
walkthrough: Both minus signs matter: get one wrong and the height comes out negative.

questions.text: A student calculates the acceleration of a braking car and gets −3 m/s². Explain what the minus sign means.
questions.model:
• The acceleration is in the opposite direction to the car's velocity (the direction chosen as positive).
  • So the car is slowing down: it is a deceleration of 3 m/s² — its velocity decreases by 3 m/s every second.

questions.text: A car travelling at 10 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 8 s.

parts.text: Calculate its final velocity.
parts.hint: You have u, a and t: v = u + at.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the distance it travels in the 8 s.
parts.hint: Now you know u, v and a; use v² − u² = 2ax (or the area under a v–t graph: a trapezium with sides 10 and 26 and width 8).
parts.label: b

sections.title: Resultant force → acceleration, and terminal velocity
sections.blurb: Two forces, one resultant, then F = ma. And the story of a falling object: the acceleration shrinks while the speed keeps growing.
checklist: Find the resultant of two opposing forces, then use it in F = ma (not one of the forces on its own)
Work out the weight first when one of the forces is gravity
Describe and explain the motion of a falling object up to terminal velocity
Say which way the acceleration points at the top of a throw

parts.title: Resultant first, then F = ma
parts.html:
$F = ma$ only works with the resultant force. If a question gives a driving force and a friction force, or a weight and an air resistance, subtract to find the resultant before dividing by the mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant.

If one of the forces is gravity and the question gives a mass, you must calculate the weight yourself: $W = m \times g$ with $g = 10$ N/kg.

The falling object (skydiver, raindrop, feather in air):

StageForcesResultantMotion
Just releasedWeight down; air resistance zero (not yet moving)= weight, downwardsAccelerates at 10 m/s²
Speeding upAir resistance grows as speed grows, but is still less than weightSmaller, still downwardsStill speeding up, but with a decreasing acceleration
Terminal velocityAir resistance = weightZeroConstant velocity (Newton's first law)

Students lose the mark by writing "the object slows down" in the second stage. It does not: as long as the resultant force points down, the speed is still increasing. It is the acceleration that gets smaller.

At the top of a throw the velocity is zero for an instant, but the acceleration is still $10$ m/s² downwards — gravity has not switched off.

parts.title: A skydiver part-way down
parts.question: A skydiver has a mass of 70 kg. At one moment the air resistance on him is 300 N. Calculate his acceleration at that moment. (g = 10 N/kg.)
steps: Weight first: $W = m \times g = 70 \times 10 = 700$ N, downwards.
Resultant force $= 700 - 300 = 400$ N, downwards (weight is bigger, so he is still speeding up).
Less than 10 m/s² because air resistance is already taking some of the weight; as he speeds up further this acceleration will shrink to zero.

questions.text: A 1500 kg car has a driving force of 4500 N. Friction and air resistance total 1500 N. Calculate the car's acceleration.
questions.hint: Resultant = 4500 − 1500, then divide by the mass.

questions.text: An 80 kg skydiver experiences 800 N of air resistance. Which statement is correct?
options: She is accelerating downwards at 10 m/s²
She is falling at a constant velocity
questions.explain: Her weight is 80 × 10 = 800 N, equal to the air resistance. Resultant force zero → constant velocity. This is terminal velocity.

questions.text: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Describe and explain how her velocity changes from the moment she jumps until she reaches terminal velocity. (Do not consider the parachute.)
questions.model:
• At first only her weight acts (air resistance is zero because she is not yet moving), so the resultant force is large and she accelerates at 10 m/s².
  • As her velocity increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force (weight − air resistance) decreases.
  • Her acceleration therefore decreases — but she is still speeding up, because the resultant still acts downwards.
  • Eventually air resistance equals her weight. The resultant force is zero, so her velocity stops changing: she falls at a constant (terminal) velocity.

questions.text: A model rocket of mass 100 kg produces a thrust of 1.5 kN upwards. Calculate its acceleration at launch. (g = 10 N/kg.)
questions.hint: Thrust up, weight down. Find the weight, then the resultant.

questions.text: A lift of mass 600 kg is pulled upwards by a cable with a tension of 7200 N. Calculate the lift's acceleration.
A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its flight, what is its acceleration? (Ignore air resistance.)
options: Zero, because it is momentarily at rest
It depends on how hard it was thrown
questions.explain: Gravity acts all the time. The velocity is zero for an instant, but the resultant force (the weight) is still there, so the acceleration is still 10 m/s² downwards.

sections.title: Core practical: the analysis
sections.blurb: Why the masses move from trolley to hanger, how two light gates give an acceleration, what friction does to the graph, and what the gradient means.
checklist: Calculate an acceleration from two light-gate readings and the time between them
Explain why the total mass must stay constant when investigating force
Explain how to compensate for friction, and how friction shows up on the graph
Interpret the gradient and intercept of an acceleration–force graph

parts.title: From light-gate times to an acceleration
parts.html:
With two light gates the data logger (or you) does three calculations:

  1. Speed at gate 1: $v_1 = \text{card length} \div \text{time through gate 1}$.
  2. Speed at gate 2: $v_2 = \text{card length} \div \text{time through gate 2}$.
  3. Acceleration: $a = (v_2 - v_1) \div \text{time to travel from gate 1 to gate 2}$.

Keep the units straight: card length in metres, times in seconds.

Why the masses move from the trolley to the hanger. The hanging weight accelerates the whole system — trolley plus hanging mass — because they are joined by the string. If you simply added more mass to the hanger you would increase the force and the mass at the same time, so you could not tell which caused the change in acceleration. Moving a mass from the trolley to the hanger changes only the force; the total mass is unchanged.

Friction. Friction on the trolley opposes the motion, so the resultant force is less than the hanging weight. Two ways to deal with it:

  • Compensate: tilt the runway slightly, until the trolley (given a gentle push, with no hanging mass) runs at a constant speed. The component of its weight down the slope now cancels friction.
  • Or leave it and read it off the graph: uncompensated friction gives an acceleration–force graph that is still a straight line, but it cuts the force axis at a positive value. That intercept is the friction force — the force you need before the trolley accelerates at all.

The gradient. From $F = ma$, $a = F \times \dfrac{1}{m}$, so the gradient of $a$ against $F$ is $\dfrac{1}{m}$: the reciprocal of the total mass. A plot of $a$ against $m$ (force constant) is a curve, because $a = F \div m$; to get a straight line, plot $a$ against $\dfrac{1}{m}$.

parts.title: Acceleration from two light gates
parts.question: A 10 cm card on a trolley takes 0.050 s to pass through the first light gate and 0.025 s to pass through the second. The trolley takes 0.4 s to travel between the gates. Calculate its acceleration.

questions.text: A trolley carries an 8 cm card. It takes 0.040 s to pass the first light gate and 0.020 s to pass the second, and 0.5 s to travel between the gates.

parts.text: Calculate the speed at the first gate.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the speed at the second gate.
parts.hint: Same card, shorter time.
parts.label: b

questions.text: A student investigates how acceleration depends on force. Explain why she moves masses from the trolley onto the hanger, rather than adding new masses to the hanger.
questions.model:
• The hanging weight accelerates both the trolley and the hanging masses, because they are connected.

• Remove the hanging mass and give the trolley a gentle push.
  • Raise the end of the runway (tilt it) a little at a time,
  • until the trolley moves along it at a constant speed (the light gates can check this).
  • The component of the trolley's weight down the slope now balances friction, so the hanging weight is the resultant force.

A curve, because a = F ÷ m

sections.title: Planning a practical: the 6-mark method question
sections.blurb: "Describe how you would investigate…" is worth six marks and most students get two. The same seven steps answer every version of it.
checklist: Pick out the two variables a "describe a method" question is asking about
Name the formula that links them
Say which variable you change, how you change it, and what you keep the same
Say which variable you measure, how, and with what equipment
Say what you will do with the results (a calculation or a graph)
Give one specific detail that makes the results accurate
Say you will repeat the readings and calculate a mean (both halves, or no mark)

parts.title: Seven steps, every time
parts.html:
Whenever a question says describe how you would investigate, plan an experiment or design a method, write your answer in these seven steps, in this order. Each step is a mark, and examiners are looking for exactly these things.

  1. Read the question, and write down the two variables you are being asked to investigate. One is the thing you will change (the independent variable); the other is the thing you will measure (the dependent variable).
  2. Figure out which formula links them. Write it down. It tells you what else must be kept the same, and what to do with the results at the end.
  3. Say which one you will change and how you will change it — e.g. "add masses to the trolley". Give a range or a number of values ("five different masses"), and say what you will keep the same so it is a fair test.
  4. Say which one you will measure, and how you will measure it, including the equipment to use — e.g. "record the speed at each light gate, and measure the distance between them with a ruler".
  5. Say what you will do with the result — e.g. "use $a = F \div m$ to calculate the acceleration" or "plot a graph of $F$ against $a$ and calculate the gradient".
  6. Add a detail about the practical to make sure you get accurate results — e.g. "release the trolley from the same point each time", "keep the ramp at the same angle", "use light gates rather than a stopwatch so there is no reaction time". One specific, relevant detail is enough.
  7. Say you will repeat the readings and calculate a mean. Both halves are needed: writing "repeat the experiment" on its own does not get the mark — you must also say that you will calculate a mean of the repeats.

Write the steps as numbered points, not as one paragraph. A labelled diagram of the equipment is worth adding if you have time, but it does not replace the words.

parts.title: Where the marks go missing
parts.html: The two most common ways to lose marks are describing the equipment without saying what you measure with it ("use light gates" earns nothing; "use light gates to record the speed at each point" does), and stopping after you have collected the data. The question asked how you would investigate the link between the two variables, so the calculation or graph that shows the link is a mark in its own right. And the easiest mark on the paper is the one most often thrown away: "repeat" alone scores nothing — "repeat and calculate a mean" scores.

parts.title: Investigating force and acceleration
parts.question: Describe how you would investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force acting on it. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — the two variables. I am investigating force (independent variable, the one I change) and acceleration (dependent variable, the one I measure).
Step 2 — the formula. They are linked by $F = m \times a$. That means the mass must be kept constant, and at the end I expect $a$ to be proportional to $F$.

Step 3 — what I change and how. The force is the weight of a mass hanging on a string that runs over a pulley to the trolley. I change the force by moving a slotted mass from the trolley to the hanger, so that the total mass being accelerated stays the same. I use five different forces.

Step 4 — what I measure and how. I put a card of known length on the trolley and set up two light gates connected to a data logger. The data logger records the speed at each gate and the time to travel between them. I measure the distance between the gates with a metre rule.

Step 5 — what I do with the results. I calculate the acceleration with $a = (v - u) \div t$ from the two speeds and the time between the gates, then plot a graph of $a$ against $F$. A straight line through the origin shows that $a \propto F$; the gradient is $1 \div m$.

Step 6 — accuracy. I release the trolley from the same marked point each time, and I tilt the runway slightly first so that the trolley runs at a constant speed with no hanging mass — this compensates for friction, so the hanging weight is the only resultant force.
Step 7 — repeat and mean. I repeat the readings for each force three times and calculate a mean acceleration for each force before plotting.

As it would be written in the exam: seven numbered sentences, one per step — about ten lines. Every sentence contains either a variable, a piece of equipment and what it measures, or what is done with a number.

parts.title: Planning a practical
parts.intro: Write the full answer on paper, as seven numbered points, before you open the mark scheme. Then mark yourself one mark per row — the question is out of six, so any six of the seven rows score.

questions.text: A student has a trolley, a set of slotted masses, a mass hanger, a string and pulley, a card, two light gates and a data logger. Describe how the student could investigate how the acceleration of the trolley depends on its mass. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any six of the seven.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the mass of the trolley is changed (independent) and the acceleration is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $F = m \times a$ (or $a = F \div m$).
3ChangeChanges the mass by adding slotted masses to the trolley, using at least five different masses, and keeps the force the same by leaving the same mass on the hanger every time.
4MeasureMeasures the acceleration using the card and two light gates with a data logger: speed at each gate, time between the gates, $a = (v - u) \div t$ (or the data logger calculates it).
5Use the resultPlots a graph of acceleration against mass (or against $1 \div \text{mass}$) and describes the link — $a$ decreases as $m$ increases; $a$ against $1/m$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $F$.
6AccuracyOne specific detail that makes the results accurate: releases the trolley from the same marked point each time, or tilts the runway to compensate for friction, or measures the card length precisely with a ruler.
7Repeat & meanRepeats the readings for each mass and calculates a mean. "Repeat" on its own does not score.
  • "Use light gates" on its own does not earn the Measure mark — you must say what the light gates measure.
  • The Use the result mark needs a graph or a calculation that links the two variables, not just "record the results in a table".
questions.hint: Step 1: the variables are mass and acceleration. Which one will you add masses to change, and what must then stay the same?

questions.text: A trolley is released from rest at the top of a ramp. Describe how you would investigate how the velocity of the trolley depends on the distance it has travelled down the ramp. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any six of the seven.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the distance travelled down the ramp is changed (independent) and the velocity at that point is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $v^2 - u^2 = 2 \times a \times x$, and that $u = 0$ because the trolley starts from rest (so $v^2 = 2ax$).
3ChangeChanges the distance by moving a light gate to different positions down the ramp, measuring the distance from the release point to the gate with a metre rule, for at least five distances.
4MeasureMeasures the velocity at the gate: a card of measured length on the trolley breaks the light-gate beam, the timer records the time, and velocity $= \text{card length} \div \text{time}$.
5Use the resultPlots a graph of $v^2$ against $x$. A straight line through the origin shows that $v^2 \propto x$ (the acceleration is constant); the gradient equals $2a$, so the acceleration is half the gradient.
6AccuracyOne specific detail that makes the results accurate: releases the trolley from the same marked point each time without pushing it, or keeps the ramp at the same angle throughout, or measures the distance to the gate from the front of the card.
7Repeat & meanRepeats the readings at each distance and calculates a mean velocity. "Repeat" on its own does not score.
  • Plotting $v$ against $x$ and saying "it curves" earns the graph part of the last mark only if you say the curve shows $v$ is not proportional to $x$; the full mark needs $v^2$ against $x$.
  • A stopwatch instead of a light gate is accepted for the Measure mark only if you say what distance and time you would use to find the velocity, and note that reaction time makes it less accurate.
questions.hint: Which equation has velocity, distance and no time in it? What does it say you should plot to get a straight line?

sections.title: Measuring reaction time
sections.blurb: The ruler-drop test and the computer test: how each works, the maths that turns a drop distance into a time, and why neither is quite the same as reacting while driving.
checklist: Describe the ruler-drop and computer-click methods of measuring reaction time
Convert a ruler-drop distance into a reaction time using x = ½gt²
Evaluate the methods: repeats, anticipation, and the difference from a real driving situation

parts.title: Two methods
parts.html:
Ruler dropComputer test
A partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero level with your open thumb and finger. Without warning they let go; you catch it as quickly as you can. Read the distance it fell. Repeat several times and take a mean.A program shows a signal (a colour change, a sound) at a random moment; you click or press a key as fast as you can. The computer records the time directly, in milliseconds. Repeat and take a mean.
Gives a distance; you convert it to a time.Gives the time directly, more precisely.

Converting the drop distance. The ruler falls freely from rest, so with $u = 0$ and $a = g$:

$$x = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2x}{g}}$$

Use the distance in metres. A 20 cm drop gives $t = \sqrt{2 \times 0.2 \div 10} = 0.2$ s. (Edexcel do not require you to derive this; they do expect you to use it.)

Evaluating. Repeating and averaging reduces random error. Problems: the catcher may anticipate the drop (so the partner must vary the timing); the catching reaction uses the hand, whereas a driver's foot has further to move to the brake, so real braking reaction times are longer; and a test done when alert does not show the effect of tiredness, alcohol or distraction. Typical results: 0.2–0.3 s for a hand catch; 0.5–0.9 s for a driver.

parts.title: Reaction time from a ruler drop
parts.question: A student catches a dropped ruler after it has fallen 20 cm. Calculate her reaction time. (g = 10 m/s².)

questions.text: A ruler falls 45 cm before it is caught. Calculate the reaction time.
A student's reaction time is 0.25 s. How far, in cm, will a ruler fall before she catches it?
questions.hint: x = ½gt², then convert metres to centimetres.

questions.text: Explain why the ruler-drop test should be repeated several times and a mean taken.
questions.model:
• Reaction time varies from one attempt to the next (random variation).
  • Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of this random error and makes the result more reliable.
  • Any anomalous result (e.g. an anticipated catch) can be spotted and left out.

questions.text: Which is an advantage of the computer test over the ruler drop?
options: It measures the time directly and more precisely
It uses a longer reaction time
It measures the driver's braking time exactly
questions.explain: The computer times the response in milliseconds with no conversion needed. It still needs repeats, and it is still a hand response, not a foot-on-brake response.

questions.text: In a ruler-drop test, student A catches the ruler at 15 cm and student B at 30 cm. Which statement is correct?
options: A has the slower reaction time
B has the slower reaction time
They have the same reaction time
B's reaction time is exactly twice A's
questions.explain: A longer drop means the ruler fell for longer before it was caught — a slower reaction. Because x ∝ t², doubling the distance makes the time √2 ≈ 1.4 times longer, not twice.

questions.text: Give two reasons why a reaction time measured by the ruler-drop test may not be the same as a driver's reaction time on the road.
questions.model:
• The catcher may anticipate the drop, giving an unrealistically short time.
  • A driver must move a foot to the brake pedal, which takes longer than closing a hand.
  • The test is done while alert and expecting a signal; a real driver may be tired, distracted or not expecting a hazard.
  • (Any two.)

sections.title: Estimation questions
sections.blurb: "Estimate the force on…" means: choose sensible values, say what you chose, calculate, and round. The method earns most of the marks.
checklist: Estimate the size of an everyday acceleration
Estimate the force in a typical road situation, stating the values you assume
Give an estimate to one or two significant figures with a unit

parts.title: How to answer an estimation question
parts.html:
An estimation question is marked on your method and sensible values, not on hitting one exact number. The examiner wants to see:

  1. Assumed values, written down with units — a mass, a speed, a time or distance. Use the typical values from the non-negotiables.
  2. The equations you are using.
  3. The calculation, to 1 or 2 significant figures.
  4. A sense check: compare the force with a weight, or the acceleration with $g$.
Useful assumed values
Mass of an adult70 kg
Mass of a car1000–1500 kg
Town speed (30 mph)13 m/s
Motorway speed (70 mph)30 m/s
Time for a car to pull away to 30 mphabout 5 s
Time to stop in a crashabout 0.1 s (0.5 s with a crumple zone)
Driver's reaction time0.7 s

Any answer within a factor of two or so of the examiner's will be accepted if your assumptions are stated and sensible. An unexplained number on its own is not.

parts.title: Estimating a crash force
parts.question: Estimate the force on a driver when a car travelling in town crashes into a wall.
steps: Assume: driver's mass $\approx 70$ kg; town speed $\approx 13$ m/s (30 mph); the driver stops in about $0.1$ s.
Sense check: about 13 times the driver's weight (700 N) — easily enough to cause serious injury, which is why cars have crumple zones and airbags.

parts.title: Estimation
parts.intro: Answers within about 20% of the model values are accepted — the method matters more than the exact number.

questions.text: Estimate the acceleration of a car pulling away from traffic lights and reaching the 30 mph limit.
questions.hint: 30 mph is about 13 m/s; a car takes roughly 5 s to get there.
walkthrough: Assume $v = 13$ m/s reached in $t = 5$ s from rest.
$a = \dfrac{13}{5} \approx 2.6$ m/s² — a few m/s², well under $g$.

questions.text: Estimate the force on a 60 kg bus passenger when the bus brakes sharply from 10 m/s to rest in 0.5 s.
questions.hint: Deceleration first, then F = ma.
walkthrough: $F = 60 \times 20 = 1200$ N — about twice her weight, which is why standing passengers get thrown forwards.

questions.text: Which is the best estimate of the force on a 1000 kg car during a motorway crash lasting 0.1 s?
questions.explain: a ≈ 30 ÷ 0.1 = 300 m/s², so F ≈ 1000 × 300 = 300 000 N. Thirty times the weight of the car.

questions.text: Describe how you would estimate the force on a cyclist who rides into a wall.
questions.model:
• Assume sensible values: the cyclist's mass (about 70 kg) and a typical cycling speed (about 6 m/s).
  • Assume a stopping time (around 0.1 s) or a stopping distance.
  • Calculate the deceleration from a = (v − u) ÷ t (or v² = 2ax), then the force from F = ma.
  • State the answer to 1 or 2 significant figures and compare it with the cyclist's weight.

questions.text: A sprinter crosses the finish line at 10 m/s and comes to a stop in about 2 s. Estimate her deceleration.
questions.hint: Change in speed ÷ time.

questions.text: Estimate the thinking distance of a car travelling at 30 mph in town.
questions.hint: 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s; a typical reaction time is about 0.7 s.
walkthrough: Thinking distance $= 13 \times 0.7 \approx 9$ m — matching the Highway Code's 9 m.
